name: Dakelh
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gessner, Suzanne C. 2003. The prosodic system of the Dakelh (Carrier) language. PhD dissertation, University of British Columbia (Lheidli dialect, Prince George; three speakers; instrumental study). Open-access UBC cIRcle item 1.0091378 (the Internet Archive capture).
catalog_locator: Abstract p.ii; sec. 2.6 p.27; sec. 2.14 'Verb stem stress and weight' p.51 (p.63); sec. 3.7 pp.141-142; sec. 3.8 p.142; sec. 3.10 p.156; sec. 3.15 'Chapter summary' pp.182-183 (p.194); sec. 5.1 p.254.
catalog_quote: [p.ii] One of the findings is that in addition to word-final stress in verbs, manifested primarily in terms of duration, "prominence" in the form of increased pitch is typically also found on one of the earlier syllables in the word. The location of the latter is partly determined phonologically, and in part lexically; certain prefixes appear to carry lexical tone ... [p.27] The stem, therefore, is always the last syllable in the word, unless there are any relativizing suffixes present. ... [p.51] For Dakelh, I will argue that verb stem syllable is stressed. This stress is realized by increased duration. ... [p.182] First of all, Dakelh does indeed seem to have both stress and tone, which appear to operate independently of each other. Stress is manifested as increased duration, and can be observed on verb stem syllables. As was argued in chapter 2, this is the head syllable of an obligatory uneven iamb (a bisyllabic light-heavy sequence), aligned with the right edge of the stem. Tone, which is entirely independent of this stress, is manifested by raised pitch. ... Every word appears to have at least one high-toned syllable (but see chapter 4 for systematic exceptions). All monosyllabic words (nouns) therefore have high tone. In bisyllabic nouns the location of high tone appears to be contrastive. Verbs, and deverbal nouns, generally have tone on their first or second syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Southern Carrier (sout2958) is not in the catalog. Of the three title hits, only Gessner 2003 (UBC dissertation, Lheidli dialect, instrumental) is about this language; it was already held by the project and was re-read: verb stress is fixed on the stem = word-final syllable and cued by duration (uneven iamb at the right edge of the stem), while a separate culminative high tone (pitch), partly lexical, falls usually on the first or second syllable of verbs and is contrastive in bisyllabic nouns; nouns show pitch prominence only (pp.51, 147, 156, 182, 254). The two Bouavichith items (2013 Phonetica; 2014 NYU) are American-English lenition studies attached to Southern Carrier by Glottolog's automatic keyword assignment from 'intervocalic' (confirmed on the Glottolog records and the Crossref abstract) — irrelevant, priority none. Side probe: the ANLC WP2 URL for Gessner 2002 (two-dialect prosody comparison) still serves a UAF 404 page despite a 200/application-pdf header; ANLA API returns nothing for it; Bird 2002 (Arizona repository) still could not be reached by automated download. New files saved: glottolog_ref_313745/601117/; appended.

Locators verified against the PDF itself with per-page extracted text: p.3 carries printed 'ii' and the Abstract; p.63 carries printed '51' and the heading '2.14 Verb stem stress and weight'; p.194 carries printed '182' and the sentence 'Dakelh does indeed seem to have both stress and tone'; p.266 carries printed '254' and 'stress and tone co-occur as independent properties'; chart (25) sits on p.142 (between the '141' and '142' foot markers). Quote check: the p.ii passage (the text) matches the report word for word, including 'certain prefixes appear to carry lexical tone, as in many related langua…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (cued by vowel duration) falls on the verb-stem syllable, which is the final syllable of the verb (and of deverbal nouns); it is the strong member of a light-heavy iamb aligned with the right edge of the stem. Independently of this, every word carries one high tone (culminative H, partly lexical, on certain prefixes), realised as a pitch peak on an earlier syllable in verbs and on either syllable of bisyllabic nouns. Alternative coding: tone language with a stress statement (Gessner treats Dakelh as a combined stress + tone system).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress stated. Instead a separate pitch prominence (H tone): in polysyllabic (deverbal) nouns usually one prefix syllable is prominent by raised pitch (and some duration), preferentially on incorporated lexical items, lexically toned morphemes, closed syllables and full vowels (pp.141-142).
new_statements.exceptions: Mono- and bisyllabic nouns show only pitch prominence, not durational stress; in bisyllabic nouns the location of H is contrastive (HL, LH, HH; p.142, p.182). Bird 2002 (per Gessner p.105) found most Lheidli bisyllables (79/111) with initial 'stress' cued by pitch and amplitude, not duration. Generalisations for prefix prominence are called preliminary (p.142).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolation/citation forms elicited from three Lheidli speakers; verbs and deverbal nouns vs. underived nouns treated separately; sentence-level prosody and tone sandhi handled in separate sections (3.3, ch.4).
new_statements.identity_note: Statement describes the Lheidli dialect (Lheidli T'enneh, Prince George), which Poser 1999b / YDLI / Gessner 2003:3 place in the Fraser-Nechakoh group of the Southern subgroup of Dakelh (= ISO caf Southern Carrier, Glottolog sout2958). Glottolog 5.3 lists only Blackwater Carrier (blac1272) as a named dialect child of sout2958, so the Lheidli assignment rests on the ISO/Poser classification, not on a Glottolog dialect node. Central Carrier carr1249 (Nak'azdli/Stuart Lake; Story 1989, Pike 1986, Walker 1979, Morice 1932) is a separate catalog entry already; no first-hand stress description of the Blackwater/Ulkatcho dialects was found (Poser's Ulkatcho and Saik'uz materials are silent on stress and tone).

new_statements.reading: Lheidli (Southern Carrier): verbs have fixed stress on the stem syllable, which is always the final syllable of the verb (p.156), cued by vowel duration (stem 140 ms vs prefix 102 ms, p<.0001, p.147) and analysed as a right-aligned uneven iamb; a separate culminative H tone (pitch), lexically specified on some morphemes and otherwise phonologically placed, sits usually on the first or second syllable of verbs and is contrastive in bisyllabic nouns; nouns of one or two syllables show only pitch prominence, no durational stress. So: fixed final (stem) stress in verbs plus an independent lexical/pitch accent H tone — a mixed stress-tone system, not a free-stress one. Earlier sources relayed by Gessner agree on final/stem stress (Morice 1932:7, Story 1984:24, Prunet 1990, Story 1989:100), while Bird 2002:92 found predominantly initial pitch/amplitude prominence in Lheidli bisyllables (79/111).
